title: What are the three delivery semantics (at-most-once, at-least-once, exactly-once), and what causes each?
shortTitle: The three delivery semantics in Kafka (at-most-once, at-least-once, exactly-once)
topicTitle: What are the three delivery semantics

s1_definition.profdef: Delivery semantics describe the guarantee a messaging system makes about how many times a message is delivered and processed in the presence of failures. At-most-once means each message is delivered zero or one time, so messages may be lost but never duplicated. At-least-once means each message is delivered one or more times, so messages are never lost but may be duplicated. Exactly-once means each message is effectively processed one and only one time, with neither loss nor duplication. In Kafka, the semantic you get is determined by how you configure producer acknowledgments and retries, and when and how the consumer commits its offsets relative to processing.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India mailing transaction receipts to Rajesh. At-most-once is like mailing a receipt and never following up — if the post loses it, Rajesh simply never gets it, but he will never get two. At-least-once is like mailing a receipt and re-sending if unsure it arrived — Rajesh definitely gets it, but he might receive duplicates. Exactly-once is like a careful system where Rajesh gets the receipt once and only once, no matter what goes wrong — never lost, never duplicated. For money, that last guarantee is the most valuable and the hardest to achieve.
s1_definition.oneliner: At-most-once may lose but never duplicate, at-least-once may duplicate but never lose, and exactly-once does neither.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Delivery semantics describe the guarantee a messaging system makes about how many times a message is delivered and processed in the presence of failures. At-most-once means each message is delivered zero or one time, so messages may be lost but never duplicated. At-least-once means each message is delivered one or more times, so messages are never lost but may be duplicated. Exactly-once means each message is effectively processed one and only one time, with neither loss nor duplication. In Kafka, the semantic you get is determined by how you configure producer acknowledgments and retries, and when and how the consumer commits its offsets relative to processing.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India mailing transaction receipts to Rajesh. At-most-once is like mailing a receipt and never following up — if the post loses it, Rajesh simply never gets it, but he will never get two. At-least-once is like mailing a receipt and re-sending if unsure it arrived — Rajesh definitely gets it, but he might receive duplicates. Exactly-once is like a careful system where Rajesh gets the receipt once and only once, no matter what goes wrong — never lost, never duplicated. For money, that last guarantee is the most valuable and the hardest to achieve.

**One line to remember:** At-most-once may lose but never duplicate, at-least-once may duplicate but never lose, and exactly-once does neither.

sections.s2_technical:
The semantic is decided at two points: the producer side and the consumer side. On the producer side, the acks setting and retry behavior determine whether a record can be lost or duplicated during sending. On the consumer side, the order of committing the offset relative to processing the record determines whether a record can be lost or reprocessed after a crash.

At-most-once happens when you commit or acknowledge before you have safely processed. On the consumer side, if a consumer commits its offset immediately after receiving a record but before processing it, and then crashes, the record is considered done and is never reprocessed, so it is lost. On the producer side, acks=0 means the producer fires and forgets without waiting for the broker, so if the send fails the record vanishes. At-most-once is fast and has the least overhead, but it tolerates loss, which is acceptable only for data you can afford to drop, like some metrics.

At-least-once happens when you process first and commit afterward. On the consumer side, the consumer processes the record and only then commits the offset; if it crashes after processing but before committing, the record is redelivered after restart and processed again, causing a duplicate. On the producer side, acks=all with retries means a record that was actually written but whose acknowledgment was lost gets resent, creating a duplicate on the broker. At-least-once never loses data, which is why it is the common default, but the application must tolerate duplicates. In Spring you get this by disabling auto-commit and committing manually after processing: `enable.auto.commit=false` and acknowledging in the listener after the work is done.

Exactly-once is the strongest and requires coordinated features. On the producer side, idempotence (`enable.idempotence=true`) makes the broker detect and discard duplicate sends from retries using a producer id and sequence numbers, so a retried write is not stored twice. On top of that, Kafka transactions let a producer write to multiple partitions and commit the consumer offsets atomically, so either everything commits or nothing does. For stream processing that reads from Kafka and writes back to Kafka, setting `processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2` in Kafka Streams gives end-to-end exactly-once. The key limitation is that true exactly-once is native to Kafka-to-Kafka flows; when the side effect is an external system like a database, you achieve effectively-once by making the consumer idempotent, for example using a unique transfer id so a reprocessed record has no second effect.

The causes, summarized in plain terms: at-most-once is caused by committing or acknowledging before processing, or acks=0. At-least-once is caused by committing after processing, or acks=all with retries, without duplicate suppression. Exactly-once is caused by combining idempotent producers, transactions, and either Kafka Streams exactly-once or an idempotent consumer for external writes.

The senior-level nuance is that exactly-once has real costs — transactions add latency and throughput overhead, and they only cover Kafka-internal writes. In most banking systems the pragmatic and robust choice is at-least-once delivery plus an idempotent consumer, which gives effectively-once results for database writes without paying the full transactional price everywhere. You reserve full Kafka transactions for genuine Kafka-to-Kafka pipelines where atomic multi-partition writes and offset commits are needed. Choosing the right semantic per use case — metrics can be at-most-once, transfers must be at-least-once with idempotency or exactly-once — is the real skill.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India processes different kinds of events and must pick the right delivery semantic for each, proving the behavior under a crash.

Problem 1 — A dashboard metric stream can tolerate losing a few points during a crash because the numbers refresh constantly. This is exactly at-most-once — commit before processing, favor speed, accept loss.

Problem 2 — A transfer event must never be lost, but the system can handle seeing it twice as long as the second time has no effect. This is exactly at-least-once plus idempotency — process then commit, and guard with a unique transfer id.

Problem 3 — A Kafka-to-Kafka enrichment pipeline that reads raw transfers and writes enriched transfers must neither lose nor duplicate within Kafka. This is exactly exactly-once with idempotent producer and transactions.

The mini-project simulates the three semantics. We build a `Message` domain object, a `Consumer` with three strategies — at-most-once (commit then process), at-least-once (process then commit), and exactly-once (idempotent process with a processed-id guard) — and a `CrashScenario` that interrupts processing to reveal loss, duplication, or neither. The demo runs each strategy through a crash and logs the outcome.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is one message TXF-1 for account SAV2001, amount 50000, processed under each of the three semantics with a crash.

Step 1 — Under at-most-once, the consumer commits the offset for TXF-1 first, marking it done, and then crashes before actually processing it. On restart, the offset is already past TXF-1, so it is never reprocessed. The message is lost. No duplicate is possible, but the debit never happened.

Step 2 — Under at-least-once, the consumer processes TXF-1 first, actually debiting the account, and then crashes before committing the offset. On restart, because the offset was not committed, Kafka redelivers TXF-1 and the consumer processes it again, causing a duplicate debit. Nothing is lost, but the account is debited twice.

Step 3 — Under exactly-once, the consumer uses the same process-then-commit flow but adds an idempotency guard keyed by the transfer id. It processes TXF-1 once, records the id, and crashes before committing. On restart, Kafka redelivers TXF-1, but the guard sees the id was already processed and ignores it, so there is no second debit. Nothing is lost and nothing is duplicated in effect.

Step 4 — The logs show the message lost under at-most-once, duplicated under at-least-once, and processed exactly once in effect under the idempotent exactly-once approach, directly demonstrating what causes each semantic and why banking uses at-least-once with idempotency for money.

```
2026-10-24 20:36:00 [INFO] [at-most-once] commit offset for TXF-1 (before processing)
2026-10-24 20:36:00 [SEVERE] [at-most-once] CRASH before processing TXF-1 -> message LOST (never reprocessed)
2026-10-24 20:36:00 [INFO] [at-least-once] processed TXF-1 SAV2001 50000 (debited SAV2001)
2026-10-24 20:36:00 [SEVERE] [at-least-once] CRASH before commit TXF-1 -> will be REDELIVERED (duplicate)
2026-10-24 20:36:00 [WARNING] [at-least-once] REDELIVERED TXF-1 SAV2001 50000 -> processed AGAIN (DUPLICATE debit!)
2026-10-24 20:36:00 [INFO] [exactly-once] processed TXF-1 SAV2001 50000 (debited once)
2026-10-24 20:36:00 [SEVERE] [exactly-once] CRASH before commit -> will be redelivered
2026-10-24 20:36:00 [INFO] [exactly-once] REDELIVERED TXF-1 -> idempotent guard IGNORES it -> NO duplicate effect
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Message TXF-1 (debit SAV2001 50000)
    │
    ├─ AT-MOST-ONCE ─────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │   commit offset → CRASH → (never processed) → LOST       │
    │
    ├─ AT-LEAST-ONCE ────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │   process (debit) → CRASH before commit → REDELIVER      │
    │   → process AGAIN → DUPLICATE debit                      │
    │
    └─ EXACTLY-ONCE (effectively) ───────────────────────────┐
        process (debit, record id) → CRASH before commit       │
        → REDELIVER → id already seen → IGNORE → single effect  │

  Cause map:
    commit BEFORE process / acks=0        → at-most-once (loss)
    process BEFORE commit / acks=all+retry→ at-least-once (dup)
    idempotent producer + txn / id guard  → exactly-once (neither)
```

```
  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────────┐
  │AtMostOnce    │  │ AtLeastOnce      │  │ ExactlyOnce          │
  │Consumer      │  │ Consumer         │  │ Consumer             │

  └──────────────┘  └──────────────────┘  │ - processedIds:Set   │
                                           └──────────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: a message under crash ──────────────────────

  AMO:  [COMMITTED] → crash → [LOST]
  ALO:  [PROCESSED] → crash(before commit) → [REDELIVERED] → [DUPLICATE]
  EO:   [PROCESSED+ID SAVED] → crash → [REDELIVERED] → id seen → [IGNORED]

  ── Call Chain (Main Scenario) ─────────────────────────────────

  1. amo.consumeWithCrash(TXF-1) → commit → crash → LOST
  2. alo.consumeWithCrash(TXF-1) → debit → crash → redeliver
  3. alo.consumeAgainAfterRestart(TXF-1) → DUPLICATE debit
  4. eo.consumeWithCrash(TXF-1) → debit + save id → crash
  5. eo.consumeAgainAfterRestart(TXF-1) → id seen → IGNORE

  Contract for exactly-once consume:
    Pre:  message has a stable unique id
    Post: processed effect applied at most once
    Rule: redelivery with a known id is a no-op
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Delivery semantics describe how many times a message is delivered and processed when failures happen, and there are three. At-most-once means a message is delivered zero or one time — it can be lost but never duplicated. At-least-once means a message is delivered one or more times — it is never lost but can be duplicated. Exactly-once means a message is effectively processed one and only one time — neither lost nor duplicated.

The semantic is decided at two points. On the producer side, the acks setting and retries decide whether a send can be lost or duplicated. On the consumer side, the order of committing the offset relative to processing decides whether a crash loses or reprocesses a record. At-most-once is caused by committing before processing, or acks=0 — you crash and the record is marked done without being handled, so it is lost. At-least-once is caused by processing first and committing afterward, or acks=all with retries — a crash between processing and committing causes redelivery, so the record is handled twice. Exactly-once is caused by combining an idempotent producer, which suppresses duplicate sends, with transactions that atomically commit writes and offsets, or Kafka Streams exactly-once for Kafka-to-Kafka flows.

The crucial real-world caveat I always give is that true exactly-once is native only to Kafka-internal flows. When the side effect is an external database, you achieve effectively-once by making the consumer idempotent, for example using a unique transfer id and a database unique constraint so a reprocessed record simply has no second effect.

In my banking platform at National Bank of India, I choose the semantic per use case. Dashboard metrics can be at-most-once because they refresh constantly and losing a few points is harmless. Transfers must never be lost, so I use at-least-once — process then commit, acks=all — paired with an idempotent consumer keyed by the transfer id, which gives effectively-once results so Rajesh is never double-debited even if a message is redelivered after a crash. For genuine Kafka-to-Kafka enrichment pipelines I use full exactly-once with idempotent producers and transactions. The senior insight is that exactly-once has latency and throughput costs and only covers Kafka writes, so for most banking cases the robust, pragmatic choice is at-least-once plus idempotency rather than paying the full transactional price everywhere.
